overview: Goguryeo was the largest and most militaristic of Korea's Three Kingdoms, controlling territory from northern Korea into Manchuria. Its tomb murals provide vivid evidence of a vibrant culture that influenced both Korean and Japanese art.

items.text: Tomb murals depict hunting scenes, processions, celestial beings and daily life with dynamic movement.
Gold crowns and jewelry show sophisticated metalworking techniques.
Buddhist sculpture and temple construction flourished after the religion was introduced in 372.
Advanced fortress construction with stone walls adapted to mountainous terrain.
Iron weapons and armor production supported large cavalry forces.
Buddhism introduced from Former Qin China, becoming a major state religion.
Native shamanistic beliefs coexisted with Buddhism and Confucianism.
Goguryeo tomb complexes are recognized as UNESCO World Heritage sites.
The kingdom's name is the origin of the English word Korea.

fall.text: After decades of warfare with Silla and Tang China, Goguryeo fell when its capital Pyongyang was captured in 668.
